chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: Settling into Le Ruban Bleu and living in Harlem
summary: Joined in 1942 after the Carter tour; the club was on East 56th Street; she lived on Conklin Avenue and her money was in escrow.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Okay. So eventually then you settled down into Le Ruban Bleu?
About 1942 when I came off the road with Benny, yeah.
And can you tell us something about that?

Yeah you know, I feel that the tour with Benny was booked through another agency and they too were, the Gale Agency, they were selling bands. And I felt that I wasn't going to get the kind of, what can I say, the treatment as an individual artist, as a featured artist if I was going to be booked through an agency that was handling bands. So when I came off the

road with Benny I went into the Rue Ban Blue. In fact, I was among some of the first acts that went into the Le Ruban Bleu. Herbert Jacoby who had a Club in Paris, the? du Trois, came over and opened the Le Ruban Bleu and it was one of the first supper clubs that was opened in the City.

It was 4 East 56th Street. And I happened to have been downtown somewhere and Jacoby and Jimmy Daniels who had worked for him, happened to be at the same place at the same time. I know what, they were going to do a picture of a composit picture of what was going on in New York at the time for Esquire Magazine. And they had some girls there from Billy Roses cabaret and so Jacoby, Jimmy Daniels and I happened to be there at the same time so we were in the montage also. And that's when I met him and he opened the Le Ruban Bleu a few months afterwards and I went in there. And that was quite a relief for me because I had been on the road for a long time and I had been through all these headaches, you know, with the management, with Claude, with Gladys, and the Columbia Artists, and all this. I had a terrific

overhead by the time I got through. My money was being held in escrow in lieu of a settlement with Claude and Gladys. So my contract with Columbia was terminating and we had broken up with Claude and I found myself free, you know, for a change. And so when I went into the Le Ruban Bleu it seemed to me from an economic standpoint that I had the better of the deal because I didn't have any overhead except what it cost me to get home each night, get to work and get home each night. And the regular things.
Where were you living at that time?

I was living in Harlem. I was living on Conklin Avenue. And so I went into the Le Ruban Bleu and decided that this was for me. And of course, you know, over a period of six years I was at the Le Ruban Bleu. And then after I left the Le Ruban Bleu I went into the Village Vanguard and I was in and out of there for four years. So I was pretty much established and I didn't have all the headaches that I would have had, had I stayed out there, sort of, what you say, in front. But in the meantime allot of people
